spans.s:
Dvādaśa, ‘consisting of twelve,’ is used of the year in the Rigveda (vii. 103, 9). See nakṣatra.
Foot notes Cf. Oldenberg, Zeitschrift der Deutschen Morgenländischen Gesellschaft, 48, 645 et seq.

Dvār is frequently used from the Rigveda onwards to denote the ‘door’ of a house. The later form, dvāra, has the same sense. Cf. gṛha. The ‘door-fastener’ is called Dvārapidhāna in the Śatapatha brāhmaṇa.
Foot notes i. 13, 6.
Av. viii. 3, 22; xiv. 1, 63; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxx. 10; Śatapatha brāhmaṇa, xi. 1, 1, 2; xiv. 3, 1, 13, etc.
Śatapatha brāhmaṇa, i. 6, 1, 19; iv. 3, 5, 9; 6, 7, 9; xi. 4, 4, 2, etc. Av. x. 8, 43, has nava-dvāra, ‘having nine openings,’ of the body.
xi. 1, 1, 1. Cf. dvāra-bāhū, ‘doorposts,’ in Lāṭyāyana śrauta sūtra, i. 3, 1; ii. 3, 9.
Dvāra-pa, ‘door-keeper,’ is only found in a metaphorical sense in the aitareya brāhmaṇa (i. 30), where Viṣṇu is called the ‘doorkeeper’ of the gods, and in the Chāndogya upaniṣad (iii. 13, 6).
